title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The experiment used a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was produced per pair by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performed structured workflow- and intent-constraint checks and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We expand artifact-grounded methodology, add per-topology accounting and compact execution metadata, clarify the degenerate bootstrap behavior, and discuss construct and external validity limits grounded in the archived run artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration commands, promising efficiency gains for NetOps. However, syntactically plausible commands can violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing a hazardous uplink switchover), cause regressions, or otherwise produce semantic failures that only closed-loop execution can detect. Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated prior to enactment. Evaluating such guarded pipelines requires executable tests that detect semantic/network-level errors beyond token- or syntax-level correctness.

We preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and executed a paired experiment that isolates whether an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy changes outcomes when the generator output is held constant across conditions. The core question: Does integrating an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting identical LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? The paired shared-generation design fixes generator variability to measure the marginal effect of the validator and repair subsystem. The present manuscript reports artifact-grounded execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact confirmatory inference, and an interpretation of the degenerate ceiling outcome observed.
sections.related_work: Two strands of prior work motivate our design. First, executable verification and closed-loop benchmarking for network configuration (e.g., recent executable testbeds and NetOps benchmarks) show that textual or syntactic checks miss sequencing and availability invariants that only emulation reveals. These studies demonstrate examples of make-before-break errors, ordering violations, and group-availability regressions that lead to operational outages when enacted without validation. Second, a growing literature on tool‑augmented LLM agents advocates generate→validate→repair architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canary deployments, translation-to-formal-model) to reduce operational risk in agentic NetOps. Survey and benchmark reports conclude that verification or executable validation materially improves detection of semantic errors, but systematic closed-loop, cross-model evidence under identical harnesses is limited. Our experiment complements this prior work by isolating the validator/repair effect using an executable emulator and a preregistered paired protocol, thereby offering a mechanistic lens distinct from generator‑variance studies.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1. The confirmatory design was paired-binary with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically partitioned into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks per class. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified confirmatory test was the exact two-sided McNemar. Complementary reporting included a bootstrap-percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729. The preregistration specified exclusion and contamination rules, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, and a missingness policy that distinguishes technical/instrumentation failures from scientific outcomes.

Task generation and task schema. Tasks were deterministically produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest contains structured fields: initial_state, expected_final_state, intent (natural-language), required_sequence (canonical command ordering that the validator enforces), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level). These structured payload fields enable the deterministic emulator validator to apply policy checks as formal constraints rather than heuristic string matches. Representative manifest entries for tasks 000001–000006 (archived) show canonical required_sequence patterns such as shutdown→mtu/vlan→restore and make-before-break uplink switchover.

Shared-generation paired design. For each pair the pipeline produced a single shared initial candidate using the declared hosted model gpt-5-mini; the execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}. Each shared candidate was evaluated twice: once under a baseline workflow (LLM-only suggestion semantics, scored by the emulator post-hoc but without repair) and once under the guarded workflow (validator may trigger at most one repair iteration if violation_count>0). This design isolates validator/repair effects on identical generator outputs and therefore measures the marginal utility of validation/repair for fixed generator behavior. The trade-off is that if the generator produces mostly valid candidates under the frozen prompt, repair is not exercised and the confirmatory test will be uninformative with respect to repair efficacy on independent generator errors.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator that applies task-encoded workflow policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator executes the candidate in an emulated environment and emits structured validator_trace fields: validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one repair iteration, invoked only when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and repair_provider_traces are archived when generated. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 and repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes.

Instrumentation, contamination controls, and deterministic reconciliation. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets between tasks (container image checksums + deterministic seeds) and recorded provider-call audits and cache statistics (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120). Contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse) were applied; no contamination flags occurred. The final deterministic_reconciliation artifact reports planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, complete_pair_count = 120, and consistent pair accounting (n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0). All instrumentation logs and checksums are archived in the execution manifest.

Statistical procedures and degenerate-bootstrap clarification. The preregistered primary test is the exact two-sided McNemar on paired binary success/failure labels. The complementary bootstrap-percentile CI resampled paired tables to derive a 95% interval for the paired-difference estimate (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). When the empirical contingency table contains zero discordant pairs (n_10 = n_01 = 0), every bootstrap resample reproduces the identical paired table and the paired-difference remains constant at 0.00; therefore the percentile CI is degenerate with zero width, which is an expected consequence of the observed concordance rather than an implementation artifact.

Representative validator diagnostics and repair activity. Because no violations were detected in any guarded episode, no repair_provider_trace artifacts were produced and preregistered secondary endpoints related to repair incidence are vacuous in this run; the absence of repair activity is an empirical result documented in the archived traces.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The paired shared-generation design was chosen to measure the validator/repair subsystem's marginal effect on identical generator outputs. Under the frozen prompt and generator settings, the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator for all 120 tasks; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and therefore could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling.

Implications for experimental design. The observed ceiling highlights a methodological trade-off: the shared-generation paired design improves internal validity for isolating validator effects by removing generator variance, but it risks generating degenerate confirmatory outcomes when the generator produces near‑perfect candidates for the chosen task corpus. For future confirmatory demonstrations of repair utility we recommend one or more of the following artifact-grounded alternatives, each supported by fields available in the archived manifest: (a) independent generation per condition so the guard can intercept natural generator errors; (b) controlled prompt perturbations (the preregistration included two perturbation variants per task as an exploratory axis) to raise generator error incidence while preserving structured task constraints; or (c) stratified selection of tasks with metadata indicating high difficulty (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) to preferentially exercise repair paths. The archived task difficulty metadata can be used to select such strata reproducibly.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, provider-call audits, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator's policy encoding being derived from synthetic task payloads; the validator enforces an explicit, reproducible policy set but may not capture vendor heterogeneity or timing constraints found in production. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power calculations assumed baseline failure ≈0.40 and targeted absolute reduction 0.15; with an observed baseline of 0.00 these assumptions fail and the confirmatory test cannot address the originally targeted effect size.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (which rules were checked, which fields were touched, and why a repair was not applied) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts demonstrate end-to-end instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) that can be repurposed for operator-facing explanations and third-party audit in production deployments where generators sometimes err. The structured validator_trace fields provide a minimal machine-readable basis for integrating operator dashboards or external audits without exposing raw provider logs.

Design recommendations for future work. (1) Replace or supplement the shared-generation protocol with independent generation per condition or controlled prompt perturbations to ensure the guard is exercised; (2) permit multi-iteration repair budgets and archive repair traces to analyze repair convergence; (3) evaluate multiple generator families under the same executable harness to measure cross-model generality; (4) expand emulator fidelity to multi-vendor behavior and partial observability; (5) develop production-rooted incident corpora with verifiable ground truth to improve external validity. The archived manifests and difficulty metadata provide concrete handles (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) to select tasks more likely to expose generator failures.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline to an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit well-defined follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
